tagline.text: A castle for the Virgin Mary on a hilltop, drawing prayers and candlelight

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 per person (day trip from Cebu City)

items.credit: Elmer B. Domingo / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons
Jennifer Bauzon / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: About 55km south of Cebu City, a Marian pilgrimage church rises on a Sibonga hilltop like a castle out of a European fairy tale. Stories of a weeping Marian statue's miracles draw pilgrims from across the Philippines, and the countless candles and thank-you letters left behind convey the intensity of the devotion here.

Simala Shrine sits on Lindogon Hill in Barangay Simala, Sibonga, in southeastern Cebu Island. Its formal name is the Monastery of the Holy Eucharist, and because it houses an image of Our Lady of Lindogon, locals commonly call it Simala Church or Simala Shrine. It lies about
55km
from Cebu City along the southern coastal road, roughly
1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours 30 minutes
by car, so many travelers stop by on trips through southern Cebu.
The shrine's story actually begins on Luzon. After Mount Pinatubo erupted in
, the Marian Monks of Eucharistic Adoration, based in Pampanga, relocated to Cebu, and in

they built a monastery on this hill. That same year, when dengue fever swept through the village, the Marian statue was said to have shed tears, and reports spread that the outbreak subsided afterward — drawing the first waves of pilgrims. Further reports of the statue weeping followed over the years; the church has not formally certified these as miracles, but among the faithful the stories carry on as an article of belief.

What began as a modest chapel has grown, through years of donations, into a vast castle-like structure of pointed spires, rounded domes, and layered arched cloisters. Terraced gardens, ponds, and fountains surround the building, and the inner cloisters are packed with letters, photographs, crutches, wheelchairs, and even diplomas left by people who say they were healed — a vivid sense of what this place means to the faithful. Construction continues in various corners even now, so the shrine looks slightly different with every visit.

For Catholic visitors, it's a place of prayer and gratitude; for non-religious travelers, it's a fascinating window into the intensity of Filipino folk devotion and its distinctive architecture. There's no entrance fee and the walking distances are short, making it a comfortable stop for family trips with elderly parents, and it pairs naturally with Carcar's lechon and a southern Cebu day trip that includes Oslob or Moalboal.

The white walls, spires, and golden domes viewed from the garden below the hill are Simala's signature image. Frame the shot with the pond and a small gazebo in front for a fairy-tale-castle photo. The white walls shine brightest when morning light hits them.

A steady line of quiet worshippers forms before the statue of Our Lady of Lindogon above the main altar. Even if you're not religious, take a moment to sit and feel the solemn atmosphere. Please keep conversation to a minimum and silence your phone.

In the offering area on one side of the shrine, you can buy candles in different colors according to your wish — health, family, studies, employment, and so on each have their own meaning — for around
each. The sight of hundreds of candles burning together is striking.

blocks.title: Touring the Gallery of Thank-You Letters

children.text: The cloisters and exhibit rooms display letters, photos, medical records, crutches, and more left by people who say they were healed or passed an exam. It's the clearest window into how closely faith is woven into daily life in the Philippines.

You can slip a written wish into petition boxes placed around the shrine. Petition slips are available near the entrance and gift shop; write your name and prayer, and the monks are said to include it in Mass.

The terraced gardens beneath the castle are dotted with ponds, fountains, and statues, ideal for a slow walk. Climb to the upper terrace for a view over the whole shrine and the green hills of Sibonga beyond.
Mass is usually held around midday on weekdays and on weekends, with a special Mass on the
13th
of every month that draws a much larger crowd of pilgrims. Mass times can change, so check the latest schedule before visiting.

At the Simala turnoff, switch to a habal-habal or tricycle up to the shrine entrance
Check attire, enter, and pray and light candles before the Marian statue in the main church
Tour the gallery of thank-you letters, the gardens and ponds, and the upper terrace
Snack at entrance stalls, browse rosaries and religious items at the gift shop
Head to Carcar for lechon lunch, then return to Cebu City
Depart Cebu City by vehicle toward Oslob
Whale shark watching in Oslob (confirm current operating details)
Head north and arrive at Simala Shrine
Worship and stroll the gardens at the shrine
Lechon and chicharon lunch in Carcar, browse the old mansion district
Arrive back in Cebu City (timing varies with traffic)

Southern Cebu's road gets more congested as the afternoon goes on, and Oslob's whale shark watching only runs early in the morning, so it's more efficient to travel in the order Oslob, then Simala, then up through Carcar.
Manila to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
, and direct flights from Incheon or Busan in Korea take about
4 hours 30 minutes to 5 hours
From the airport to Simala is about
65km
, roughly
2 to 2 hours 30 minutes
by car. The bridge linking Mactan Island to mainland Cebu and the Cebu City downtown stretch can get congested, so leave with plenty of time to spare.
At Cebu City South Bus Terminal (CSBT), board a Ceres bus headed toward Sibonga, Argao, Dalaguete, or Oslob, and ask the driver to let you off at the Simala turnoff. It takes about
1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours 30 minutes
, and the fare is about
Air-conditioned vans (V-hire) also depart near the same terminal; they're a bit faster than the bus but have less luggage space.
From the coastal-road turnoff up to the shrine entrance on the hill is about
10–15 minutes
by habal-habal, at about
per person. Chartering a tricycle costs about
On the way back, catch a habal-habal waiting near the shrine entrance down to the coastal road to flag a bus toward Cebu City. Buses can run full past by late afternoon, so don't leave it too late.
Chartering a vehicle with a driver for the day from Cebu City or Mactan costs about
. If you're traveling with a group or combining Simala with Oslob and Carcar, this is by far the most convenient option.
A one-way trip by Grab or taxi costs about
, but it can be hard to catch a ride back from the shrine, so it's better to negotiate a round-trip rate with waiting time included. Parking at the shrine costs about
Southern Cebu is driest during
December–May
, and
January to April
especially brings clear skies that make the white walls stand out most. At midday in
April and May
, though, temperatures climb to
, making the outdoor gardens and stairs tiring, so an early morning arrival is best. During the
June–November
rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and the southern coastal road may be restricted when a typhoon passes through.
The shrine itself is open year-round, but on the
13th

of every month, on weekends, during Holy Week, and around Christmas, pilgrim crowds swell and the lines for entry and parking grow long. For a quiet visit, a weekday morning is best. Opening hours generally run around
8 AM to 5 PM
, but they can shift for events or construction, so check the latest notices.

There are only a few small lodgings for pilgrims near Simala, so most people stay in Cebu City or Mactan and visit as a day trip. Cebu City accommodation ranges from business hotels at about
a night to large hotels above
. If you're also visiting Oslob or Moalboal, staying at a beach resort there and stopping by Simala en route is another good option.
Food isn't allowed inside the shrine grounds, and stalls and small restaurants selling snacks and drinks cluster just outside the entrance. For a proper meal, head to Carcar, about
20–30 minutes

north — famous for Cebu-style whole roast pig lechon, crispy pork rind chicharon, and sweet peanut brittle ampaw, it's a common lunch stop for Filipinos after a Simala pilgrimage too. Back in Cebu City, you'll find seafood restaurants and sutukil grills to enjoy.
The dress code is very strict. Wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and avoid sleeveless tops, shorts, and short skirts. Men in shorts will also be turned away at the entrance.

If your outfit doesn't meet the code, shawls and wrap-skirts can be borrowed or bought near the entrance, but the line can get long on busy days, so it's easier to simply wear long clothing from the start.
Visiting on a weekday morning means fewer people, so you can pray quietly before the Marian statue and take photos at a relaxed pace. It's best to avoid the 13th of the month and weekends.
Eating, drinking, and smoking are prohibited inside the shrine, and photography is restricted in some areas. Follow the posted signs and staff instructions.
Candles, petition slips, and donations are cash only. Bring plenty of small bills.
There are many stairs and slopes, and the marble floors can be slippery, so comfortable low-heeled shoes are best. Wheelchair users should confirm accessible routes before visiting.
Combining Simala with Oslob's whale sharks, Carcar's lechon, and Osmeña Peak makes for a well-rounded day in southern Cebu — a chartered vehicle with driver is the most efficient way to do this.
Entry is refused if the dress code is violated. Be sure to cover your shoulders and knees, and don't speak loudly or run inside the shrine.
On days with large pilgrim crowds, the entrance and offering area get very congested. Keep your phone and wallet in a bag worn in front.
Touts near the entrance may try to sell religious items or candles at inflated prices. Use the official stalls and confirm prices first.
The outdoor gardens and stairs offer little shade at midday. Bring a hat and water, and watch for heatstroke.
Do not touch the Marian statue, the altar, or the displayed testimonial items, and avoid using flash photography or taking selfies in front of people who are praying.
It can be hard to catch a bus to Cebu City from the coastal-road turnoff late in the afternoon. Arrange your return transport in advance.
